sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of systems will bring widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and increase the potential for coastal flooding along with high surf throughout much of the upcoming week. Guidance is hinting at the development of upper-level ridging towards the end of the week but uncertainty remains in its amplitude and exact placement.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Wednesday night)
paragraphs: Shower coverage is becoming sparse across the region this afternoon. However, a 965 mb surface low and its associated frontal boundary will lift widespread rainfall across the region, starting at the coast by the evening before spreading inland as the night progress. Snow levels will rise, ending the winter weather advisory for the Olympics but they are to stay low enough over higher Cascade passes. As a result, a winter weather advisory remains in effect for the North Cascades through Tuesday night. Surface gradients tighten as gusty SE winds is forecast for portions of the area. The strongest winds will be over the San Juan and Island counties and along the coast where the probability for gusts over 40 MPH exceed 80%. Wind advisories are in effect along the coast. Overnight lows range between the upper 30s to mid 40s.

The frontal system will round out of the region Tuesday evening but lingering showers and breezy winds are forecast to remain. It'll only clear the runway for yet another disturbance to track into the region on Wednesday night into early Thursday with yet another round of widespread rainfall and breezy winds. Snow levels look to be well above pass level by Wednesday evening as any precipitation that's slated to fall will be liquid. In addition to periods of widespread precipitation and gusty winds, coastal flooding and high surf will also be of concern. High surf along the pacific in concert with high tides will combine to lead to hazardous conditions along the coastline this eek including both major coastal flooding and high surf. Conditions will likely peak on Tuesday and last into the latter half of the week. Tides will also cause concern for inland coastlines starting Wednesday. A flurry of coastal flood advisories/warning and high surf advisories are in effect. Temperatures throughout the short-term will rise above average with highs in the lower to mid 50s and lows well into the 40s.

sections.title: Long term (Thursday through Monday)
paragraphs: Thursday's frontal system will push off and away by the evening but it won't go away without the concern for additional impacts. Models are signaling at yet another round of gusty winds and periods of widespread rainfall possibly moderate to heavy at times. High surf and coastal flood impacts will also peak on Thursday. Active conditions will linger into Friday but guidance is beginning to signal at a building upper-level ridge over the weekend. Confidence lacks in its intensity and exact placement but brief pattern change may be on the horizon. Temperatures will return closer to average Friday onwards.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: VFR all areas currently. However, the next system will bring more widespread rain this evening into early Tuesday. Visibility reductions down to MVFR are possible with the heaviest bands of rain. Mountains likely see lower ceiling obstructions. Southeast winds will continue, with most seeing 5-10 kt but isolated gusts up to 20 kt have been observed. Gusts may top out near 30 kt at KHQM late tonight into early Tuesday. Winds aloft will be stronger and out of the southwest, so there will be some potential for wind shear (especially Tuesday morning). Periods of rainfall likely into Tuesday with continued breezy winds.

KSEA...Confidence is leaning towards mostly VFR ceilings throughout much of the upcoming period. However, the NBM is hinting at 30% chance of MVFR conditions are possible overnight into early Tuesday morning under heavier rainfall. Winds out of the south- southeast 8-15 kt with gusts near 20 kt at times. Rainfall will begin at the terminal between 00z-06z Tuesday and last before breaking into showers later on Tuesday.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system will remain offshore for much of the week, with several fronts moving over area waters. The first frontal passage associated with this system is crossing the waters today, with a slew of headlines across the waters. A Storm Warning remains in effect over the outer coastal waters, with Gale Warnings in place for both the west and east entrances of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Small Craft Advisories also remain in effect for the central Strait of Juan de Fuca, the northern inland waters, and for Grays Harbor Bar. Winds will remain elevated throughout the evening and overnight areas for most locations, with a brief lull over the central Strait before picking back up again Tuesday.

The system offshore will continue to bring elevated winds across area waters, with headlines likely to continue well into the week. Gusty winds will continue on Tuesday, and another frontal passage Wednesday into Thursday will bring in a round of potentially even stronger winds over area waters. This will likely bring additional Storm Warnings over the outer coastal waters, with potential for small crafts to gales for most other areas. As this system continues to influence the area, isolated thunderstorms remain possible each afternoon, mainly over the coastal waters.
High pressure is favored to build over the region by Friday, bringing a brief break from winds before additional systems bring widespread elevated winds by next week.

Seas around 10 to 15 feet this afternoon will continue to build to 18 to 25 feet by Tuesday afternoon. Seas will ease slightly over the outer waters Wednesday and Thursday, though wave period will increase by a few seconds, bringing long period swells. Seas will gradually ease throughout the day Friday, falling below 10 feet overnight into Saturday. However, that is expected to be short- lived, with seas building to 8 to 12 feet by the end of the weekend.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region through this week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely reach flood stage around midweek and topping into moderate, possibly near major given latest guidance. A river flood watch has been issued for Mason County from Wednesday morning through Sunday afternoon.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active Pacific weather pattern is expected through this week, bringing a series of wet and progressively warmer systems across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington. Rain spreads along the coast this afternoon, with light rain pushing inland overnight as a warm front lifts northward. Rain returns Tuesday into Wednesday, but remains light. A stronger frontal system associated with atmospheric river moisture brings heavier rainfall to the area Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, along with rising snow levels and breezy winds. A potential break in precipitation may develop by Saturday as high pressure attempts to build over the region, but wet weather likely returns late this weekend.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active Pacific weather pattern is expected through this week, bringing a series of wet and progressively warmer systems across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington. Rain spreads along the coast this afternoon, with light rain pushing inland overnight as a warm front lifts northward. Rain returns Tuesday into Wednesday, but remains light. A stronger frontal system associated with atmospheric river moisture brings heavier rainfall to the area Wednesday night through Thanksgiving Day, along with rising snow levels and breezy winds. A potential break in precipitation may develop by Saturday as high pressure attempts to build over the region, but wet weather likely returns late this weekend.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Sunday...A broad low pressure system well offshore over the Pacific will slowly lift northward toward the Gulf of Alaska today through Wednesday. The bulk of the moisture is expected to remain offshore, with rain spreading to the coast and Coast Range tonight as the warm front lifts north. Some light rain may also clip portions of the inland valley tonight, with highest chances (20-40%) for 0.10 inch of rainfall from Salem northward. By Tuesday morning, conditions likely trend drier, though briefly as rain returns with a cold front pushing onto the coast. The upper level trough weakens as it moves over the Pacific NW Tuesday night, followed by a band of rain showers moving onshore. In general, 48- hour total precipitation amounts through Wed afternoon are expected to be highest along the coast and Coast Range, with ensemble and NBM guidance suggesting at least a 50% chance of anywhere from 0.5 inch to 2.0 inches of accumulation. Total rainfall accumulation east of the Coast Range through Wed afternoon is expected to be much less, at around 0.25 inch or less, except across southwest Washington where there is a 30-40% chance of exceeding 0.50 inch.

An offshore pressure gradient today through Tuesday will also produce breezy east to southeast winds, including at the coast and across the Portland Metro area. With high pressure building east of the Cascades and low pressure over the Pacific, the pressure gradient between KTTD and KDLS has increased to around -6 mb. East winds are currently gusting up to  25-35 mph across portions of the eastern Portland metro this afternoon. Latest model guidance suggests the pressure gradient strengthens to around -7 to -8 mb by Tuesday morning which would likely increase gusts up to 40 mph. Probabilities for widespread gusts exceeding 45 mph are currently 30% or less in the eastern Portland metro, so will hold off from issuing a wind advisory at this time.

The next weather system will approach the region later Wednesday likely spreading more widespread rain across the area through Thanksgiving Day. There is increasing potential for a moderate to strong Atmospheric River to develop with this system as the associated moisture plume becomes oriented more west-southwesterly and IVT values peak around 750 kg/ms at the coast and near 500 kg/ms into the foothills. Rainfall amounts will depend on where the initial frontal band makes landfall and duration as it sags southward across the region. The range of total accumulations remains large (as indicated between the 10th and 90th percentiles), but mean 24-hour values indicate potential for 1 to 2 inches along the coast and terrain, as well as into the Cascades and foothills; while there is anywhere from a 30-60% chance of exceeding 1.0 inch within the Willamette Valley and closer to a 50-80% chance for the south WA lowlands.

Gusty south winds are also expected to develop along the coast Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. With potential for a coastal jet to set up, winds may gust as high as 50-65 mph, strongest for beaches and headlands. There is currently around a 30- 50% chance for wind gusts exceeding 58 mph along the coast, but lower chances (15-30%) for high winds reaching the inland communities.

Concerns for travel through the Cascade passes is minimal through at least Friday, and likely the weekend, as snow levels are expected to rise from around 6000 ft on Tuesday to around 7,000-8,000 ft on Thursday as the warm sector lifts into the area ahead of the atmospheric river. This will bring above average temperatures along with the rainy and cloudy conditions to much of the region.

Uncertainty increases heading into the weekend as clusters show differences between locations of the Pacific trough and western US ridging. The majority of solutions (at least 60%) do show the ridge shifted more west, keeping the more active weather farther offshore. This trends well with a lower probability of precip from the NBM (20- 40%) on Saturday. But chances for rain increase again by Sunday as clusters indicate a break down of the ridge with more zonal flow to troughing approaching the coast.  /DH

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Wednesday...VFR conditions are expected to prevail across the region tonight through Tuesday. Late this afternoon, radar and satellite observations show a weak frontal boundary shifting towards the region increasing light rain/showers this evening, especially along the coast. At least the persistent offshore flow should keeps CIGs AOA 4kft. Once this frontal feature passes, activity likely decreases Tuesday morning before picking up along the coast again later Tuesday afternoon. Beyond the precipitation, the pressure gradient across the Cascades continues to tighten increasing winds along the eastern Portland Metro with gusts around to 28-38 kt at KTTD. Winds likely remain breezy/gusty through the Columbia Gorge and Cascade gaps over the next 24hr, peaking Tuesday morning, along with breezy south- southeast winds right along the coastline. Given the gusty easterly winds at the surface and more of a southerly component aloft near 2kft in the east Portland Metro, LLWS may be a concern at KPDX/KTTD.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR through the TAF period. Easterly winds continue to gust around 25-30 knots today and tonight with higher gusts closer to 35 knots near the I-205 bridge. With more of a S-SE wind at 2kft, LLWS might be concern, especially for the eastern portion of the terminal. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: The active weather pattern keeps rather hazardous marine conditions in play through the middle of the week. Our next frontal system is quickly approaching the coastline this afternoon with buoys reporting gale force wind gusts across the outer waters while more of an easterly component has kept wind gusts just under gale force criteria for the inner waters. Then tonight into Tuesday winds from the incoming system strengthen, bringing storm force wind gusts of 50-57 kt to the outer waters, mainly beyond 30-40 NM offshore. For the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, winds increase to gale force with gusts up to 35-45 knots before decreasing late Tuesday night. While we see a brief lull on Wednesday, a similarly strong front increases winds yet again Wednesday night into Thursday morning and the NBM shows a 40-70% chance for storm force wind gusts across the inner and outer waters with the second frontal system.

Seas will also gradually build into Tuesday, peaking between 17-22 ft at 15-17 seconds Tuesday afternoon. The steepest seas are expected beyond 30 NM, where there is moderate to high confidence (60-85% chance) for seas exceeding 20 ft largely due to a fresh southerly wind-wave swell. For the inner waters and the main channel of the Columbia River Bar, chances to exceed 20 ft are much lower comparatively (20-40%). Then Tuesday evening we'll likely see the arrival of a longer period (15-17 seconds) westerly swell helping to maintain seas in the 17-22ft range through Wednesday. While this swell begins to dissipate Wednesday night, another strong frontal boundary likely kicks up another fresh southerly swell into Thursday morning keeping seas elevated near 20ft. Finally, a switch to somewhat calmer conditions. -99

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect through the middle of the week as the combination of King Tides, elevated seas, and the arrival a longer period swell likely leads to tidal overflow - impacts are most likely at high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. It's also worth highlighting the moderate to high sneaker wave threat today through Wednesday and Thursday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
